The {{Nihongo|'''Akutagawa Prize'''|芥川龍之介賞|Akutagawa Ryūnosuke Shō}} is a [[Japanese literature|Japanese]] [[literary award]] presented semi-annually. Because of its prestige and the considerable attention the winner receives from the media, it is, along with the [[Naoki Prize]], one of Japan's most sought after literary prizes.<ref name=jtfukue /><ref name=mack>{{cite journal|title=Accounting for Taste: The Creation of the Akutagawa and Naoki Prizes for Literature|last=Mack|first=Edward|journal=Harvard Journal of Asiatic Studies|date=2004|volume=64|number=2|pages=291–340|doi=10.2307/25066744|jstor=25066744}}</ref>

==History==
[[File:Ryunosuke Akutagawa 01.jpg|thumb|175px|Ryūnosuke Akutagawa, author, after whom the prize is named]]
The Akutagawa Prize was established in 1935 by [[Kan Kikuchi]], then-editor of [[Bungeishunjū (magazine)|''Bungeishunjū'']] magazine, in memory of author [[Ryūnosuke Akutagawa]].<ref name=mack /> It is sponsored by the [[Society for the Promotion of Japanese Literature]], and is awarded in January and July to the best serious [[literature|literary]] story published in a newspaper or magazine by a new or rising author.<ref name=jtfukue>{{cite web|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120215222749/http://www.japantimes.co.jp/text/nn20120214i1.html|archive-date=February 15, 2012|url=http://www.japantimes.co.jp/text/nn20120214i1.html|work=[[The Japan Times]]|title=Literary awards run spectrum|last=Fukue|first=Natsuko|date=February 14, 2012|access-date=July 27, 2018}}</ref> The winner receives a pocket watch and a cash award of 1 million yen. The judges usually include contemporary writers, literary critics, and former winners of the prize. Occasionally, when consensus cannot be reached between judges over disputes about the winning story or the quality of work for that half year, no prize is awarded. From 1945 through 1948 no prizes were awarded due to postwar instability.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.booksfromjapan.jp/awards/item/575-akutagawa-prize|title=Akutagawa Prize|work=Books from Japan|access-date=August 24, 2018|archive-date=December 15, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181215105802/https://www.booksfromjapan.jp/awards/item/575-akutagawa-prize|url-status=dead}}</ref> The prize has frequently been split between two authors.<ref name="CopelandRamirez-Christensen2001">{{cite book|author1=Rebecca L. Copeland|author2=Esperanza Ramirez-Christensen|title=The Father-Daughter Plot: Japanese Literary Women and the Law of the Father|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=M50BEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA287|date=31 July 2001|publisher=University of Hawaii Press|isbn=978-0-8248-6471-2|page=287}}</ref>

On January 15, 2004, the awarding of the 130th Akutagawa Prize made significant news when two women became the award's youngest winners.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2004/03/27/world/the-saturday-profile-just-20-she-captures-altered-japan-in-a-debut-novel.html|title=Just 20, She Captures Altered Japan in a Debut Novel|work=[[The New York Times]]|last=Onishi|first=Norimitsu|date=March 27, 2004|access-date=August 24, 2018}}</ref> The prize went to both [[Risa Wataya]], 19, for her novel {{Nihongo|''I Want to Kick You in the Back''|蹴りたい背中|Keritai Senaka}} and to [[Hitomi Kanehara]], 20, for her debut novel {{Nihongo|''[[Snakes and Earrings]]''|蛇にピアス|Hebi ni Piasu}}. In 2013 [[Natsuko Kuroda]] won the 148th Akutagawa Prize at age 75, making her the oldest recipient in the history of the prize.<ref name=kuroda>{{cite news|url=https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2013/01/17/national/natsuko-kuroda-75-becomes-oldest-akutagawa-literary-award-winner/|title=Natsuko Kuroda, 75, becomes oldest Akutagawa literary award winner|work=[[The Japan Times]]|date=January 17, 2013|access-date=August 24, 2018}}</ref>

===Controversies===
In 1972, Akutagawa winner {{ill|Akio Miyahara|ja|宮原昭夫}} was found to have committed plagiarism.<ref name=beauchamp>{{cite journal|url=http://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/ED109045.pdf|title=Modern Japanese Novels in English: A Selected Bibliography|last=Beauchamp|first= Nancy Junko|journal=Service Center Paper on Asian Studies|number=7|date=May 1974}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=Plagiarism, Hiroshima, and Intertextuality: Ibuse Masuji's Black Rain Reconsidered|author=Yi-ling Lin|url=https://reitaku.repo.nii.ac.jp/?action=repository_action_common_download&item_id=183&item_no=1&attribute_id=22&file_no=1|volume=19|number=2|page=43|publisher=麗沢学際ジャーナル (Urarasawa interdisciplinary journal)|year=2011|access-date=August 19, 2014}}</ref> In 2018, a similar controversy occurred when the candidate novel {{Nihongo|||Utsukushii Kao}} by Yuko Hojo was found to have reused text from its nonfiction source material without attribution, but the [[Society for the Promotion of Japanese Literature]] did not remove the book from the candidate list.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://mainichi.jp/english/articles/20180718/p2a/00m/0na/023000c|title=Akutagawa literary prize candidate causing stir over alleged plagiarism|work=[[Mainichi Shimbun]]|last=Ohara|first=Kazuki|date=July 18, 2018|access-date=July 27, 2018}}</ref>

===Records===

* The youngest recipient of the prize to date is [[Risa Wataya]] who was 19 when she received the award for ''I Want to Kick You in the Back'' ({{Nihongo|2=蹴りたい背中|3=Keritai Senaka}}). 
* The best-seller title (in Japan only) is ''[[Spark (Matayoshi novel)|Spark]]'' ({{Nihongo||火花|Hibana}}), by [[Naoki Matayoshi]] which sold 2,29 millions of copies.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-08-13 |title=又吉さん「火花」２０万部増刷、累計２２９万部 : ライフ : 読売新聞（YOMIURI ONLINE） |url=http://www.yomiuri.co.jp/life/book/news/20150811-OYT8T50041.html |access-date=2024-12-17 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150813221904/http://www.yomiuri.co.jp/life/book/news/20150811-OYT8T50041.html |archive-date=13 August 2015 }}</ref>
